full_name: Randomized Gradient Extrapolation Method (RGEM) for deterministic strongly convex finite-sum optimization
source_reference: Lan, First-order and Stochastic Optimization Methods for Machine Learning, Springer 2020 (Algorithm 5.4, Theorem 5.4)

problem.description: Deterministic finite-sum convex optimization problem treated by RGEM.

variable_space.math: X\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \text{ is a closed convex set},\quad f_i:X\to\mathbb{R},\ i=1,\ldots,m.

assumptions.name: X_closed_convex
assumptions.math: X\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a closed convex set}

assumptions.name: component_convexity
assumptions.math: f_i : X \to \mathbb{R},\ i = 1, \ldots, m,\ \text{are smooth convex functions with Lipschitz continuous gradients over } X.

assumptions.name: average_smoothness
assumptions.math: \|\nabla f(x_1)-\nabla f(x_2)\|_*\le L_f\|x_1-x_2\|\le L\|x_1-x_2\|,\quad \forall x_1,x_2\in X.

assumptions.name: strongly_convex_regime
assumptions.math: \mu\ge 0\text{ is a given constant. Hence, the objective function }\psi\text{ is strongly convex whenever }\mu>0.

assumptions.name: optimal_solution_feasible_context
assumptions.math: x^*\text{, an optimal solution of (5.2.1) (or (5.2.5)),}\quad x\text{ any feasible solution of (5.2.1) (or (5.2.5))}

assumptions.name: RGEMNonnegativeInputParameters_Algorithm_5_4
assumptions.math: \text{Let }x^0\in X,\text{ and the nonnegative parameters }\{\alpha_t\},\{\eta_t\},\text{ and }\{\tau_t\}\text{ be given.}

input.name: RGEMInput_Algorithm_5_4
input.math: \text{Let }x^0\in X,\text{ and the nonnegative parameters }\{\alpha_t\},\{\eta_t\},\text{ and }\{\tau_t\}\text{ be given.}

steps.name: component_gradient_update
steps.math: y_i^t=\begin{cases}\nabla f_i(x_i^t),& i=i_t,\\ y_i^{t-1},& i\ne i_t.\end{cases}

main_theorem.statement_math: \text{Let }x^*\text{ be an optimal solution of (5.2.1), }x^k\text{ and }\underline{x}^k\text{ be defined in (5.2.50) and (5.2.53), respectively, and }\hat L=\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}L_i.\ \text{Also let }\{\tau_t\},\{\eta_t\},\text{ and }\{\alpha_t\}\text{ be set to }\tau_t\equiv\tau=\frac{1}{m(1-\alpha)}-1,\quad \eta_t\equiv\eta=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\mu,\quad \text{and }\alpha_t\equiv m\alpha.\ \text{If (5.2.56) holds and }\alpha\text{ is set as }\alpha=1-\frac{1}{m+\sqrt{m^2+16m\hat L/\mu}},\text{ then }\mathbb{E}[V(x^k,x^*)]\le \frac{2\Delta_{0,\sigma_0}\alpha^k}{\mu},\quad \mathbb{E}[\psi(\underline{x}^k)-\psi(x^*)]\le 16\max\left\{m,\frac{\hat L}{\mu}\right\}\Delta_{0,\sigma_0}\alpha^{k/2},\quad \Delta_{0,\sigma_0}:=\mu V(x^0,x^*)+\psi(x^0)-\psi^*+\frac{\sigma_0^2}{m\mu}.
main_theorem.rate: Linear in expectation, with objective gap bounded by O(max{m, Lhat/mu} Delta alpha^{k/2}) and distance bounded by O(Delta alpha^k / mu).
main_theorem.measure: expected Bregman distance to x^* and expected objective suboptimality of the weighted output

proof.description: Set \theta_t=\alpha^{-t}, t=1,\ldots,k, as the proof does before checking the Proposition 5.6 side conditions.
Using \tau_t\equiv\tau from (5.2.76) and the weight schedule, verify the component-weight recurrence (5.2.61). This is one of the conditions the proof says is easily checked.
Using \alpha_t\equiv m\alpha from (5.2.76) and \theta_t=\alpha^{-t}, verify the extrapolation-weight relation (5.2.65).
Using \eta_t\equiv\eta from (5.2.76), \alpha from (5.2.77), and the weight schedule, verify the Bregman-telescope condition (5.2.66).
Using the constant policy (5.2.76), the definition of \alpha in (5.2.77), and \hat L=\max_i L_i, verify the cross and terminal bounds (5.2.67) and (5.2.68).
proof.produces: Derived conditions (5.2.67) and (5.2.68) for all component Lipschitz constants L_i\le\hat L.

proof.description: Collect the verified conditions (5.2.61) and (5.2.65)--(5.2.68), together with the initial-gradient assumption (5.2.56), to make Proposition 5.6 applicable under the theorem's parameter policy.
Substitute the constant parameter policy (5.2.76) into the two estimates of Proposition 5.6.
Use the observation \alpha\ge (2m-1)/(2m) to dominate the geometric factor and sum it.
proof.produces: Uniform bound on the stale-gradient geometric series.

proof.description: Combine the two substituted estimates with the geometric sum and the fact m(1-\alpha)\le 1/2.
Read the second relation in (5.2.81) as the bound (5.2.78).
Use the weighted output formula and convexity of the squared norm to bound the squared distance of \underline{x}^k by the weighted average of iterate squared distances.
proof.produces: First line of the output-distance estimate.

proof.description: Apply the Bregman lower bound (5.2.8) and the geometric sum of weights for \theta_t=\alpha^{-t}.
Use the just-proved (5.2.78) inside the weighted sum and simplify the printed finite sum.

Before applying (5.2.60), record that the output point is feasible: (5.2.50) gives x^t\in X, Algorithm 5.4 gives \theta_t>0 and the normalized formula (5.2.53), and convexity of X makes \underline{x}^k a convex combination of feasible iterates.
proof.produces: \underline{x}^k is a feasible solution of (5.2.1), so the comparison (5.2.60) may be specialized at x=\underline{x}^k.

proof.description: Specialize the generic feasible-solution comparison (5.2.60) at x=\underline{x}^k, then combine it with the Q-bound from (5.2.81) and the weighted output squared-distance estimate.

key_lemmas.name: ProxMappingInequality_Lemma_3_5
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let the convex function }p:X\to\mathbb{R},\ \tilde x,\tilde y\in X,\ \mu_1,\mu_2\ge 0\text{ be given. Let }\nu:X\to\mathbb{R}\text{ be a differentiable convex function and }V(x,z)\text{ be defined in (3.2.2). If }\hat u\in \operatorname{Argmin}\{p(u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,u):u\in X\},\text{ then for any }u\in X,\text{ we have }p(\hat u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,\hat u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,\hat u)\le p(u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,u)-(\mu_1+\mu_2)V(\hat u,u).
key_lemmas.role: Applied to the prox update (5.2.50) to produce the one-step prox inequality (5.2.71).

proof.description: Use optimality of \hat u in the prox-mapping and differentiability of V(\tilde x,\cdot).
proof.math: \langle p'(\hat u)+\mu_1\nabla V(\tilde x,\hat u)+\mu_2\nabla V(\tilde y,\hat u),u-\hat u\rangle\ge 0,\quad \forall u\in X.

proof.description: Apply the three-point identity for the Bregman distance.
proof.math: V(\tilde x,u)=V(\tilde x,\hat u)+\langle \nabla V(\tilde x,\hat u),u-\hat u\rangle+V(\hat u,u),\quad \forall u\in X.

proof.description: Expand both Bregman-distance terms around \hat u; the second center \tilde y uses the same identity as the one displayed for \tilde x.
proof.math: p(u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,u)=p(u)+\mu_1[V(\tilde x,\hat u)+\langle \nabla V(\tilde x,\hat u),u-\hat u\rangle+V(\hat u,u)]+\mu_2[V(\tilde y,\hat u)+\langle \nabla V(\tilde y,\hat u),u-\hat u\rangle+V(\hat u,u)].
proof.produces: Expanded expression for p(u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,u).

proof.description: Use convexity of p and the variational inequality for \hat u to replace p(u) and collect the first-order terms.
proof.math: p(u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,u)\ge p(\hat u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,\hat u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,\hat u)+\langle p'(\hat u)+\mu_1\nabla V(\tilde x,\hat u)+\mu_2\nabla V(\tilde y,\hat u),u-\hat u\rangle+(\mu_1+\mu_2)V(\hat u,u).
proof.produces: Intermediate lower bound with the variational inner-product term retained.

proof.description: Drop the nonnegative variational inner-product term and rearrange to the lemma's stated inequality.
proof.math: p(u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,u)\ge [p(\hat u)+\mu_1V(\tilde x,\hat u)+\mu_2V(\tilde y,\hat u)]+(\mu_1+\mu_2)V(\hat u,u).

key_lemmas.name: GeneralRGEMBound_Proposition_5_6
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let }x^t\text{ and }\underline{x}^k\text{ be defined as in (5.2.50) and (5.2.53), respectively, and }x^*\text{ be an optimal solution of (5.2.1). Let }\sigma_0\text{ be defined in (5.2.56), and suppose that }\{\eta_t\},\{\tau_t\},\text{ and }\{\alpha_t\}\text{ in RGEM satisfy }\theta_t(m(1+\tau_t)-1)=\theta_{t-1}m(1+\tau_{t-1}),\quad t=2,\ldots,k,\quad \text{and }m\theta_{t-1}=\alpha_t\theta_t,\quad t\ge 2,\quad \theta_t\eta_t\le \theta_{t-1}(\mu+\eta_{t-1}),\quad t\ge 2,\quad 2\alpha_tL_i\le m\tau_{t-1}\eta_t,\quad i=1,\ldots,m;\ t\ge 2,\quad 4L_i\le \tau_k(\mu+\eta_k),\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\quad \text{for some }\theta_t\ge 0,\ t=1,\ldots,k.\text{ Then, for any }k\ge 1,\text{ we have }\mathbb{E}[Q(\underline{x}^k,x^*)]\le \left(\sum_{t=1}^k\theta_t\right)^{-1}\widetilde\Delta_{0,\sigma_0},\quad \mathbb{E}[V(x^k,x^*)]\le \frac{2\widetilde\Delta_{0,\sigma_0}}{\theta_k(\mu+\eta_k)},\quad \text{where }\widetilde\Delta_{0,\sigma_0}:=\theta_1(m(1+\tau_1)-1)(\psi(x^0)-\psi^*)+\theta_1\eta_1V(x^0,x^*)+\sum_{t=1}^k\left(\frac{m-1}{m}\right)^{t-1}\frac{2\theta_t\alpha_{t+1}}{m\eta_{t+1}}\sigma_0^2.

proof.description: Define B_{i_t} as the event that the sampled block has never been updated until iteration t; by the point update (5.2.51), on this event x_{i_t}^{t-1}=x^0, so its probability and the initial gradient bound (5.2.56) give the displayed estimate.

Set x=x^*, using the feasible optimal-solution context for the comparator x^*. Insert the stale-gradient bound into (5.2.75), then apply Lemma 5.10 with the recurrence hypothesis supplied by (5.2.61). Combine this with nonnegativity of Q(\cdot,x^*), where the nonnegativity side uses that each x^t is feasible by (5.2.50) and that the Proposition 5.6 weights satisfy \theta_t\ge0.

proof.description: Before invoking convexity of Q(\cdot,x^*), record the admissible weighted-average structure: Proposition 5.6 supplies \theta_t\ge0, Algorithm 5.4's output clause supplies positive output weights for (5.2.53), and the normalized denominator is therefore positive.
proof.produces: \underline{x}^k is the normalized convex combination of the points x^t with admissible weights, so Jensen/convexity may compare Q(\underline{x}^k,x^*) to (\sum_{t=1}^k\theta_t)^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^k\theta_t Q(x^t,x^*).

proof.description: Use convexity of Q(\cdot,x^*) and the weighted output definition to pass from the weighted Q-sum to Q(\underline{x}^k,x^*), giving the first result in (5.2.69).
